transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2027-06-29
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortiz (Redwood SE), Liam Park (Redwood Solutions Eng); Aisha Rahman (CTO, Stonebridge), Tom Keller (Lead ML Eng), Priya Singh (Platform Eng), Ben Howard (Security)

Summary:
Redwood runthrough focused on migration playbook: mapping OpenAI/Anthropic/Together endpoints to Redwood API, routing/fallback policies, prefix/KV cache tradeoffs, canary rollouts and dedicated vs hosted performance/cost scenarios. Security and private deployment questions surfaced; team agreed to run a small benchmark and exchange artifacts.

Topics Covered:
- API parity mapping (models, params, streaming differences)
- Routing policies + fallback strategies (latency-first vs cost-first)
- Caching: prefix vs KV cache and cache invalidation patterns
- Batching and quantization recommendations per workload
- Canary rollouts, A/B, automatic fallback and observability in Console
- Security: SOC2, KMS, VPC/private control plane concerns
- Next steps: cost parity sheet, bench run, sample payload share, private deployment follow-up

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood side. Rafael and Liam are here to walk through the migration playbook. Aisha, do you want to kick us off with your priorities?
[00:20] Aisha Rahman: Yeah thanks, Maya. Main things — cost predictability, p95 latency under 200ms for our realtime routing, and auditability for regs. We're running a hybrid: Anthropic for chat, OpenAI for summarization, and Together for longer completions. Want to consolidate without regression.
[00:46] Tom Keller: And to add, we have some existing retry logic and a circuit breaker. Curious how Redwood's fallback routing would plug in.
[01:02] Rafael Ortiz: Great, that maps well to what we show. We'll demo the API mappings and then the Console routing UI. First high level — Redwood supports model variants and can route by policy (latency, cost, region, tier). For example you can say: primary is gptx-like replica (OpenAI map), fallback to a smaller quantized variant for cost during spikes.
[01:30] Priya Singh: How do you handle KV cache warmup? Our workload has a lot of repeated prefixes for shipment tracking prompts.
[01:40] Liam Park: Good question. We do prefix caching at the runtime layer and maintain per-tenant KV caches. For repeated, high-cardinality prefixes we recommend sticky routing to keep cache affinity. There's also a TTL and eviction policy you can tune.
[01:58] Ben Howard: Are keys encrypted at rest? KMS support?
[02:05] Rafael Ortiz: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for private deployments, and hosted customers can use Redwood-managed KMS with customer-managed keys in dedicated plans.
[02:22] Speaker 2: Sorry, small note — earlier you said K V cash, I think the transcript misheard.
[02:28] Maya Chen: (laughs) yeah, transcription does that. KV cache, definitely.

[02:40] Demonstration Segment — API parity mapping:
[02:40] Rafael Ortiz: Ok pulling up the parity sheet. On the left we map OpenAI params: model, temperature, top_p, max_tokens. On Redwood API we support the same semantics and also streaming with chunked deltas. Note: Together's stop-token handling differs, Redwood normalizes stop sequences but we call out where behavior diverges in the mapping doc.
[03:10] Tom Keller: Any gotchas with function-calling and structured outputs? We rely on that for our orchestrator.
[03:18] Rafael Ortiz: We support function/tool calling patterns. We surfaced a couple edge cases: Together's function call priority and Anthropic's safety envelope are different. We recommend a small eval to validate your current tool grammar.
[03:40] Aisha Rahman: Can we keep streaming behavior identical? Some clients rely on partial deltas to show typing.
[03:46] Liam Park: Yes, streaming is supported. There may be small differences in jitter; we have streaming tuning in Dedicated deployments to reduce tail latency.

[04:05] [Demonstration: Redwood Console — Routing Policies]
[04:05] Maya Chen: Switching to the Console demo. Here you see a rule engine: route by latency SLO, then by model family, then by region. You can set canary percentages and automatic fallback if p95 exceeds threshold.
[04:30] Priya Singh: If we set a fallback to a quantized model, does Redwood auto-handle token alignment so outputs remain coherent?
[04:40] Rafael Ortiz: There's an important caveat: quantized variants may produce slightly different tokens due to precision. We provide a quality monitor that runs your prompt sets and surfaces regressions. In practice for many workloads we keep prompt engineering small and it's a 0.5-2% recent difference but your mileage may vary.
[05:02] Tom Keller: Ok. How about batching — we currently already do request coalescing in our infra. Would Redwood's batching double-up?
[05:12] Liam Park: Redwood does continuous batching at the runtime. If you already coalesce, you can tune both sides. We can expose batching windows and max latency so both don't fight. Also recommended: client-level affinity + pre-queued batches for high throughput low-latency paths.

[05:40] [Timestamp jump / minor crosstalk] 
[05:52] Speaker 3 (unknown): mhm, right
[05:58] Rafael Ortiz: Quick demo of a canary: we flip 10% traffic to a lower-cost model and watch the eval metrics. Console shows token-level cost delta and p95 latency. If cost reduction exceeds X while p95 stays under threshold, canary continues; otherwise automatic rollback.

[06:30] Aisha Rahman: That rollback flow — is it hard cutover or gradual? Our infra needs graceful degradation.
[06:38] Rafael Ortiz: Gradual, you can configure burn-in, traffic ramp, and fallback e.g., immediate fallback to primary if a hard error occurs. For latency breaches we have soft-fail policies that route to a regional replica first.

[07:05] Security & Compliance Questions:
[07:05] Ben Howard: For Private deployment — how isolated is the control plane? We need audit logs retention for 18 months.
[07:14] Maya Chen: For Private, you can opt for customer-managed control plane and VPC peering or an on-prem package. Audit logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; we have a compliance add-on for extended retention. We'll attach SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow-up.
[07:35] Ben Howard: Any certifications for HSM integrations?
[07:38] Rafael Ortiz: We support standard HSM/KMS providers; specifics depend on your env. We'll pull the attestation matrix.

[08:05] Performance Deep-dive (simulated):
[08:05] Rafael Ortiz: Here's a sim where we map OpenAI gptx-8k to Redwood m8x-prod. We show median 120ms, p95 190ms on Dedicated with n1 GPUs under our config. In hosted the p95 is a bit higher. For Together-like longer generates we recommend sequence-splitting or streaming to reduce memory pressure.
[08:40] Tom Keller: Do you have example configs for autoscaling under bursty freight-tracking loads?
[08:46] Liam Park: Yes — we have autoscale policies tuned for spike profiles: target utilization + provisioned burst capacity. We'll share the policy templates.

[09:05] Cost conversation (rough math):
[09:05] Maya Chen: Using your current usage pattern we estimate a 20-35% token-cost reduction if you adopt batching + prefix caching + a mix of quantized variants for non-critical flows. The exact number depends on hit rate for KV cache and acceptance of small quality variance.
[09:28] Aisha Rahman: Interesting. We need a detailed parity and cost sheet.
[09:32] Maya Chen: Yes that's the parity-cost spreadsheet we'll send. It will map your OpenAI/Anthropic/Together calls to Redwood endpoints and show cost per 1M tokens under different configs.

[10:00] Transcript continues with technical Q&A and examples:
[10:00] Tom Keller: A couple specific implementation questions — how do we preserve request headers for attribution if routing changes mid-flight?
[10:12] Rafael Ortiz: The runtime preserves request metadata and we emit enriched traces. In Canary we attach a routing id so you can correlate traces across models.
[10:30] Priya Singh: Do you support custom tokenizers or do we need to adapt?
[10:35] Liam Park: We support standard byte-pair tokenizers and can accept custom vocab in Dedicated/Private with some onboarding work. That's a common ask for retention of tokenization parity.

[11:00] (small pause + background noise)
[11:18] Aisha Rahman: For our legal team, they'll want a redlined SLA. Who handles that?
[11:22] Maya Chen: For Dedicated/Private, our contracts team handles SLA redlines. We'll loop in Sales Ops and Legal after this call.

[11:40] Live mini-benchmark notes discussed:
[11:40] Rafael Ortiz: We'll run a 1k-request bench with your sample payloads we asked for: one chat/short completion, one long completion, and one embedding-like call. We'll compare p50/p95 and token unit cost across Hosted/Dedicated and with a quantized fallback.
[12:05] Tom Keller: Cool. We'll give you a sample histogram of request size and payload shapes.

[12:20] Mishit/Transcription artifacts: some words mis-captured (Redwood Optima -> Redwood Optimize, K V cash -> KV cache)

[12:35] Closing and Recap:
[12:35] Maya Chen: Recap — action items and next steps: we'll send parity-cost sheet and security pack today, Rafael will run bench and recommend batching/KV config, Stonebridge to share sample payload + traffic hist by Friday, then we schedule a private-deployment deep dive with Ben and infra.
[12:55] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. Tom and Priya will sync on payload. Ben will follow up on certs.
[13:05] Maya Chen: Great, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with calendar invites for the bench review.
[13:12] Meeting ends.
